b.x: 27.1 Authentication versus authorization
Authentication
Verifies identity.
Authorization
Determines permitted actions after identity is established.
27.2 DAC versus RBAC
DAC
Resource owners or authorized controllers can grant or revoke permissions.
RBAC
Permissions are grouped into roles, and users or service identities are assigned to those roles.
27.3 Data at rest versus data in transit
At rest
Data stored in files, disks, backups, snapshots, or other persistent storage.
In transit
Data moving between systems over a network.
Both need protection. Encrypting a database file does not automatically secure a remote connection, and TLS does not automatically encrypt an offline backup.
27.4 Encryption versus hashing
Encryption
Reversible with the appropriate key.
Hashing
Produces a digest and is not designed for reversal.
27.5 Auditing versus monitoring
Auditing
Creates records of events for accountability and investigation.
Monitoring
Analyzes events and metrics to detect suspicious behavior or operational problems, often in near real time.
27.6 SQL versus NoSQL
SQL relational systems
Use relational tables, constraints, and query operations that support structured relationships.
NoSQL systems
Use alternative data models and often optimize for specific access patterns, flexible records, or distributed workloads.
Neither category is universally better. Modern products may overlap in features.
27.7 MongoDB versus Cassandra
MongoDB
Document model, nested BSON records, and document-oriented queries.
Cassandra
Distributed wide-column model, partition-oriented data design, and tunable consistency.
27.8 CAP versus ACID consistency
CAP consistency
A strong distributed consistency guarantee, commonly described using linearizability, during coordination and partition scenarios.
ACID consistency
Preservation of database integrity constraints and valid business states across transactions.
These meanings should not be confused in an exam answer.
27.9 Big Data Vs
Volume
How much data.
Velocity
How quickly data arrives or must be processed.
Variety
How many formats or data types.
Veracity
How reliable the data is.
Value
How useful the results are.
27.10 Data lake versus data warehouse
Data lake
Often retains data in raw or varied formats for multiple processing uses.
Data warehouse
Usually contains curated, structured data optimized for analytics and reporting.
27.11 Database versus blockchain
Database
Usually provides controlled storage, queries, updates, and transaction management under an operator or defined administrative model.
Blockchain
Provides a replicated ledger whose accepted history is linked cryptographically and governed by a consensus or agreement protocol.

sec.s: Security labels, Bell–LaPadula, Biba, Chinese Wall and attribute-based access control compared with DAC and RBAC.

b.x: 31.1 Why go beyond DAC and RBAC?

In Discretionary Access Control (DAC) the owner of an object decides who may access it, and in Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) permissions are attached to roles. Both are flexible, but both trust ordinary users and administrators to make good decisions. A careless owner can GRANT a secret table to everyone, and a role can slowly collect more permissions than it should. Some organisations, such as defence, intelligence, banking regulators and hospital research units, cannot accept that risk. They need rules that are enforced by the system itself and that no ordinary user can override. This is the idea of Mandatory Access Control (MAC).

In this section we study MAC and multilevel security, two integrity and conflict-of-interest models, and the newer Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC), which is popular in cloud and microservice systems.
31.2 Mandatory Access Control (MAC)

In MAC the access decision is made by a central security policy, not by the owner of the data. Every subject (user, process) and every object (table, row, file) is given a security label. The system compares the labels on every request and allows or denies it. Users cannot change labels or pass on their rights, even for objects they created.

x: Subject: an active entity such as a user or a program running for a user.
Object: a passive entity such as a table, a row, a column or a file.
Clearance: the label attached to a subject, showing how trusted the subject is.
Classification: the label attached to an object, showing how sensitive it is.
Reference monitor: the trusted component that checks every access against the policy and cannot be bypassed.

b.x: 31.3 Security levels and the dominance relation

A common set of levels, from lowest to highest, is Unclassified (U), Confidential (C), Secret (S) and Top Secret (TS). Written as an order, U < C < S < TS. A label can also contain compartments (categories) such as FINANCE or HR, which limit access to people who have a need to know. A label L1 dominates L2 when the level of L1 is at least the level of L2 and the compartments of L1 include all compartments of L2.

x: (S, {FINANCE, HR})  dominates  (C, {FINANCE})
(S, {FINANCE})      does NOT dominate  (C, {HR})

b.x: 31.4 The Bell–LaPadula model (confidentiality)
Bell–LaPadula (BLP) was designed to stop secrets from leaking to people who are not cleared for them. It has two main rules.

x: Simple security property, also called no read up: a subject may read an object only if the subject's clearance dominates the object's classification.
Star property (*-property), also called no write down: a subject may write to an object only if the object's classification dominates the subject's clearance.

b.x: The second rule looks strange at first. A user with Secret clearance is not allowed to write into a Confidential file, because a careless or malicious program could copy secret information down into a place where less-cleared people can read it.

x: Clearance of Meera = Secret
Top Secret  ------  cannot read, can write (write up)
Secret      ------  can read, can write
Confidential ----- can read, cannot write (no write down)
Unclassified ----- can read, cannot write

b.x: 31.5 The Biba model (integrity)

Biba is almost the mirror image of BLP and protects integrity instead of secrecy. It says no read down and no write up: a high-integrity subject should not read low-integrity data, because it could be contaminated, and a low-integrity subject should not write into a high-integrity object, because it could corrupt it. For example, an untrusted web form (low integrity) must not be able to overwrite the payroll master table (high integrity).

x: Bell–LaPadula
Protects confidentiality. No read up, no write down.
Biba
Protects integrity. No read down, no write up.
Clark–Wilson
Protects integrity through well-formed transactions, separation of duties and audit; users act only through approved programs.

b.x: 31.6 The Chinese Wall model (conflict of interest)

The Chinese Wall model is used in consulting, auditing and investment banking. Data is grouped into company datasets, and companies that compete with each other are put in the same conflict-of-interest class. Once an analyst has read data of Bank A, he may no longer read data of Bank B in the same class, but he may still read data of an oil company. The access rights therefore depend on the history of what the user has already accessed, which neither DAC nor simple MAC can express.
31.7 Multilevel databases and polyinstantiation

In a multilevel secure database, different rows (or even cells) have different labels. A Secret user sees all rows up to Secret, while an Unclassified user sees only Unclassified rows. A problem appears when a low user inserts a row whose primary key already exists as a higher-level row. Refusing the insert would tell the low user that a secret row exists (a covert channel). Polyinstantiation solves this by letting both rows exist with the same key but different labels.

x: MISSION(Code, Target, Label)
X7 | Training exercise | U
X7 | Border operation  | S
Unclassified user sees  : X7 | Training exercise
Secret user sees both   : two different rows for key X7

b.x: Oracle Label Security and PostgreSQL with SELinux integration are examples of products that offer label-based MAC for databases. Support differs from product to product, so check the documentation of the system you use.
31.8 Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC)

ABAC decides access by evaluating a policy over attributes. The attributes can belong to four groups: the subject (department, role, clearance, employment type), the resource (owner, sensitivity, type), the action (read, update, export) and the environment (time of day, network location, device is managed or not). The policy is written as rules, for example:

x: PERMIT if
subject.department == resource.department
and subject.clearance >= resource.sensitivity
and action in {read, update}
and environment.time between 09:00 and 18:00
and environment.device_managed == true
otherwise DENY

b.x: A doctor can therefore read the records of her own hospital ward during duty hours from a hospital laptop without anybody creating a special role such as Ward7-Doctor-Daytime. This avoids the role explosion that large RBAC systems suffer from.
31.9 Policy-based access control and policy engines

Policy-Based Access Control (PBAC) keeps the rules in a central policy that is separate from the application code. A Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) intercepts the request, asks a Policy Decision Point (PDP) for a permit or deny answer, and a Policy Information Point (PIP) supplies the missing attributes. Standards such as XACML and modern policy engines follow this structure. In databases the same idea appears in row-level security policies, which are studied in the next section.

x: Model
Who decides?
DAC
The owner of the object, using GRANT and REVOKE.
MAC
The central policy, using labels and rules. Users cannot override it.
RBAC
The administrator, by assigning users to roles that hold permissions.
ABAC
A policy engine, by evaluating attributes of subject, resource, action and environment at request time.
Model
Strength and weakness
DAC
Flexible and simple, but a careless owner can leak data and Trojan horse programs can pass rights on.
MAC
Strongest control and prevents leaks, but rigid, costly and hard to administer.
RBAC
Easy to audit and matches job structure, but can suffer role explosion and cannot express context.
ABAC
Very fine-grained and dynamic, but policies are complex to write, test and audit.

Students often reverse the BLP rules. Remember: BLP protects secrets, so you cannot read up (above your clearance) and cannot write down (to a lower label). Biba protects integrity, so the directions are reversed.

A 5-mark answer on MAC should include: labels (clearance and classification), the dominance rule, the two BLP rules with one example each, and one limitation such as covert channels or administrative cost.

b.x: 32.1 Layers of defence inside the database

Earlier sections explained the theory of access control and encryption. Real systems turn that theory into concrete database features. A good design uses several layers together, because no single control is perfect. This section walks through the most useful features and shows small examples.
32.2 Views as a security tool

A view exposes only some columns or rows of a table. Users are granted access to the view but not to the base table, so they never see the hidden data. The SQL examples below use broadly standard syntax.

x: CREATE TABLE employee (
emp_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
name TEXT, department TEXT,
salary NUMERIC, national_id TEXT);
CREATE VIEW employee_public AS
SELECT emp_id, name, department FROM employee;
GRANT SELECT ON employee_public TO helpdesk_role;
-- helpdesk_role has no privilege on employee itself

b.x: Views can also filter rows, for example WHERE department = 'HR' for the HR clerk's view. Be careful, however: a poorly written view that exposes a key column or allows updates through the view may still leak or change data. Some products also provide security-barrier views so that user-written functions cannot see rows before the view's filter is applied.
32.3 Column-level privileges

x: GRANT SELECT (emp_id, name, department) ON employee TO helpdesk_role;
GRANT UPDATE (department) ON employee TO hr_clerk;
REVOKE SELECT (salary) ON employee FROM helpdesk_role;

b.x: Column privileges are supported in MySQL and PostgreSQL. SQLite has no GRANT or REVOKE at all, so in SQLite the application must enforce such rules. Always check what your DBMS supports.
32.4 Row-level security (RLS)

Row-level security lets the database filter the rows a user may see or change, based on a policy. PostgreSQL implements it with CREATE POLICY. The same table then returns different rows to different users, and even a forgotten WHERE clause in application code cannot leak other users' rows.

x: -- PostgreSQL
CREATE TABLE orders (
order_id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
customer TEXT NOT NULL,
amount NUMERIC);
ALTER TABLE orders ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY own_orders ON orders
FOR SELECT
USING (customer = current_user);
CREATE POLICY own_orders_write ON orders
FOR INSERT
WITH CHECK (customer = current_user);

b.x: USING decides which existing rows are visible, and WITH CHECK decides which new or modified rows are allowed. Table owners and superusers normally bypass RLS unless it is forced, so test the policy using an ordinary account. In multi-tenant applications the usual pattern is a tenant_id column and a policy such as USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::int).
32.5 Dynamic data masking

Dynamic data masking changes the value shown to a user at query time, while the stored value stays unchanged. A support agent may see a card number as XXXX-XXXX-XXXX-4321 and an email as a...@example.test, while an authorised fraud analyst sees the real value. Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle and several other systems offer built-in masking features, and Cassandra 5.0 added dynamic data masking. Masking is a convenience layer and not a replacement for access control or encryption, because a determined user with query rights may still infer the hidden value through filters such as WHERE salary > 50000.
32.6 Transparent data encryption versus application-level encryption

x: Feature
Transparent Data Encryption (TDE)
Where encryption happens
Inside the database engine or storage layer, on data files, logs and backups.
Protects against
Theft of disks, snapshots and backup files.
Does not protect against
A logged-in user or DBA running SELECT, or SQL injection; the engine decrypts data for any authorised query.
Application changes
None.
Feature
Application-level (field-level) encryption
Where encryption happens
In the application, before data is sent to the database.
Protects against
Curious DBAs, stolen database credentials, cloud provider access, and database memory dumps.
Cost
Harder to search, sort or index encrypted columns; the application must manage keys.
Typical use
National ID numbers, health notes, card data.

b.x: 32.7 Tokenization

Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a random token and keeps the real value in a separate, heavily protected token vault. The application stores and passes around only the token. Unlike encryption there is no mathematical way to get the original from the token. Payment systems use tokens in place of card numbers to reduce the scope of PCI-DSS audits. The DPDP Rules 2025 list virtual tokens as one example of a security safeguard.
32.8 Storing passwords correctly

Passwords must never be stored in plain text or encrypted. They are stored as a slow, salted hash. A salt is a random value stored beside the hash, unique for each user, so that two users with the same password get different hashes and pre-computed rainbow tables are useless. A pepper is an additional secret value kept outside the database, for example in a key vault. Fast hashes such as MD5 or plain SHA-256 are unsuitable, because attackers can try billions of guesses per second. Use a deliberately slow password-hashing function such as bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2.

x: import bcrypt                            # Python, pip install bcrypt
pw = b'correct horse battery staple'
hashed = bcrypt.hashpw(pw, bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
stored = hashed                           # save in the users table; the salt is inside it
ok = bcrypt.checkpw(b'guess', hashed)   # False
ok = bcrypt.checkpw(pw, hashed)         # True

b.x: 32.9 Envelope encryption

Encrypting a whole database with one master key is risky and slow to rotate. In envelope encryption each piece of data is encrypted with a Data Encryption Key (DEK), and the DEK is itself encrypted by a Key Encryption Key (KEK) kept in a Key Management Service or hardware security module. Only the wrapped DEK is stored beside the data.

x: plaintext --(DEK)--> ciphertext        stored in database
DEK       --(KEK)--> wrapped DEK       stored beside the data
KEK never leaves the KMS / HSM
Rotate KEK: re-wrap the small DEKs; no need to re-encrypt all data.

b.x: 32.10 Secrets management

x: Never hard-code database passwords in source code or commit them to Git.
Keep them in a secrets manager or environment-injected vault, and rotate them regularly.
Use separate accounts for the application, for migrations and for humans, each with least privilege.
Prefer short-lived credentials and certificate-based authentication where the platform supports them.

b.x: 32.11 Separation of duties and secure configuration

Separation of duties means that no single person can complete a sensitive task alone. For instance, the DBA who manages the server should not also be the only person who can read or delete the audit log. A hardening checklist for a database server usually includes the following.

x: Apply security patches promptly and remove unsupported versions.
Disable or remove default accounts, sample databases and unused features.
Change default ports only as a minor measure; the real control is a firewall allowing only application servers.
Do not expose the database directly to the internet.
Require TLS for all connections and verify the server certificate.
Turn on auditing for logins, privilege changes and schema changes.
Limit file-system and operating-system level access from SQL features, such as file import or shell execution functions.

b.x: 32.12 Backups, ransomware and the 3-2-1 rule

Backups are both a security asset and a security risk. They must be encrypted, access-controlled and tested. Ransomware attackers try to encrypt or delete the backups first, so at least one copy must be out of their reach. The 3-2-1 rule says: keep 3 copies of the data, on 2 different kinds of media, with 1 copy off-site. Modern practice adds immutable (write-once, retention-locked) backups and an offline or logically air-gapped copy. A backup that has never been restored in a test is only a hope, not a backup.

x: TDE is often described as 'encrypting the database', which makes students think the data is protected from every user. It is not. It protects stored files and backups only; authorised sessions still see plain text.

When asked to compare masking, encryption and tokenization, remember: masking hides at display time, encryption is reversible with a key, and tokenization replaces the value with a random token that is reversible only through the vault.

sec.t: Inference Attacks, Statistical Database Security and Privacy Techniques
sec.s: Inference and tracker attacks, anonymization, k-anonymity, l-diversity, t-closeness and the idea of differential privacy.

b.x: 33.1 The inference problem

A statistical database allows users to ask for aggregate results such as COUNT, SUM and AVG, but not for individual rows. The idea is that a researcher may learn that the average salary of a department is 55,000 without learning any single person's salary. Unfortunately, clever combinations of allowed queries can reveal individual values. This is called an inference attack. Access control alone cannot stop it, because every single query is permitted.

x: EMP(Name, Dept, Gender, Salary). Only COUNT, SUM and AVG are allowed.
Q1: SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE Dept='CS';  -> 300000
Q2: SELECT SUM(Salary) FROM EMP WHERE Dept='CS' AND Name <> 'Ravi'; -> 240000
Subtracting: Ravi's salary = 300000 - 240000 = 60000.
Each query looked harmless, but together they exposed one person.

b.x: 33.2 Defences against inference

x: Query-set-size restriction: refuse any query that covers fewer than k rows (and, for symmetry, more than N - k rows). If the rule is k = 5, a query about one named person is refused. Note that Q1 and Q2 above both cover many rows, so this rule alone does not stop them.
Query auditing: remember earlier queries and refuse a new one if the combination would reveal an individual value. This is expensive and hard to do perfectly.
Output perturbation: add small random noise to the answer.
Data perturbation or generalisation: modify the data itself before releasing it.
Partitioning: divide records into groups and allow queries only over complete groups.

b.x: 33.3 Tracker attacks

A tracker is a carefully chosen pair of queries that defeats the query-set-size rule. Suppose the system refuses any query that matches fewer than 3 records. The attacker wants to know whether a unique person, say the only female professor in a department, earns more than a given amount. Instead of asking directly, he asks queries on larger sets, such as 'all professors' and 'all professors except female ones', whose sizes pass the threshold, and then takes the difference. The tracker idea shows why simple set-size restrictions are not enough and why stronger methods are needed.
33.4 Anonymization and pseudonymization

x: Pseudonymization
Direct identifiers (name, phone) are replaced by a code. The mapping table is kept separately. The data can be linked back with the mapping, so it is still personal data under most laws.
Anonymization
The data is changed so that the individual can no longer be identified by any reasonably likely means. It cannot be reversed. Truly anonymous data is hard to achieve.
Masking
The shown value is hidden or altered for display.
Generalisation
Exact values are replaced by ranges, for example age 23 becomes 20-29.

b.x: Removing the name column is not anonymization. Attributes such as postal code, date of birth and gender are called quasi-identifiers. Combined, they can single out a person, and an attacker can match them to another public data set, such as a voter list. This is called a linkage attack. Well-known research has shown that a large share of a population can be uniquely identified by only a few such attributes.
33.5 k-anonymity

A released table satisfies k-anonymity if every combination of quasi-identifier values appears in at least k rows. Each person is then hidden in a crowd of at least k people with identical quasi-identifiers. The usual tools are generalisation (replace values by wider ranges) and suppression (remove rare rows or cells).

x: Original (quasi-identifiers: Age, PIN; sensitive: Disease)
Age  PIN     Disease
27   110013  Cancer
41   560001  Diabetes
47   560003  Cancer
3-anonymous version (Age generalised, PIN truncated)
Age     PIN     Disease
20-29   1100XX  Cancer
40-49   5600XX  Diabetes
40-49   5600XX  Cancer

b.x: Each group of quasi-identifier values has 3 rows, so the table is 3-anonymous.
33.6 Weaknesses of k-anonymity: l-diversity and t-closeness

k-anonymity protects who you are in the table but not what is said about you. Suppose all 3 rows in a group have Disease = Cancer. An attacker who knows that a neighbour belongs to that group learns that she has cancer without identifying her row. This is a homogeneity attack. A background-knowledge attack is also possible, for instance if the attacker knows that people from a certain community rarely have a given disease.

x: l-diversity: every group must contain at least l well-represented different values of the sensitive attribute. In the example above the first group (Flu, Cancer, Flu) has 2 distinct values, so that group is 2-diverse; a group with Cancer, Cancer, Cancer would be only 1-diverse and would leak the disease.
t-closeness: the distribution of the sensitive attribute inside each group must be close (within a distance t) to its distribution in the whole table. This also stops skewness attacks.

b.x: 33.7 Differential privacy

Differential privacy (DP) gives a mathematical promise: the result of a query should be almost the same whether or not any single person's record is in the database. An attacker therefore learns almost nothing about any individual, whatever extra knowledge he has. The strength of the promise is controlled by a privacy parameter ε (epsilon). A smaller ε means stronger privacy and noisier answers.

x: Pr[ M(D1) in S ]  ≤  e^ε × Pr[ M(D2) in S ]
D1 and D2 differ in one person's record

b.x: The classic way to achieve DP for a counting query is the Laplace mechanism. A COUNT changes by at most 1 when one person is added or removed, so we add random noise drawn from a Laplace distribution with scale 1/ε to the true answer. For ε = 0.5 the noise is typically a couple of units, which is small for a count of 10,000 but large for a count of 5. Every answered query uses up part of a privacy budget, and the total budget limits how many questions can be answered. Large organisations use DP when publishing statistics, such as census data or usage analytics.

x: True count of patients with condition X is 1,204.
With ε = 1 the system might answer 1,203.4 or 1,206.1, which is useful for statistics.
The same mechanism on a true count of 3 may return a value such as 1 or 5, so the answer cannot prove whether one particular person is present.

b.x: 33.8 Data minimization

The simplest privacy technique is to collect and keep less data. Collect only the fields that the stated purpose needs, keep them only as long as needed, and delete or aggregate them afterwards. Data that does not exist cannot be breached. This idea is also a legal principle in privacy laws, which section 34 discusses.

x: Do not say that pseudonymized data is anonymous. If a mapping table or another dataset can re-link it, it is still personal data.

k-anonymity hides identity, l-diversity hides the sensitive value, t-closeness limits how much the group's value distribution can differ from the whole table, and differential privacy adds calibrated noise with a provable guarantee.

sec.t: Data Protection Law and Compliance: India's DPDP Act 2023 and Rules 2025
sec.s: Roles, consent, rights, breach reporting, timeline and how privacy law shapes database design; GDPR, PCI-DSS and HIPAA in brief.

x: This section explains the ideas for a database course. Laws, rules and dates change. Always read the current text of the Act, the Rules and any official notifications before relying on any detail, especially penalty amounts and effective dates.

b.x: 34.1 Why a database student must know privacy law

Personal data is stored in databases, so the database is where privacy rules are either honoured or broken. Requirements such as 'delete the data when the purpose is over', 'prove that the user consented' and 'report a breach quickly' translate directly into tables, columns, jobs and logs. A designer who ignores them may have to redesign the system later.
34.2 India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (DPDP Act) is India's main law on processing digital personal data. It applies to personal data collected in digital form, or collected offline and then digitised, and it also covers processing outside India when it is connected with offering goods or services to people in India. The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology on 13 November 2025 to make the Act operational.

x: Data Principal
The individual to whom the personal data relates. For a child, this includes the parent or lawful guardian, and for a person with a disability it includes the lawful guardian.
Data Fiduciary
The person or organisation that decides the purpose and means of processing personal data. It carries the main duties.
Data Processor
A person who processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary, for example a cloud or payroll vendor.
Consent Manager
A registered entity through which a Data Principal can give, manage, review and withdraw consent in one place.
Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF)
A fiduciary notified by the government because of factors such as the volume and sensitivity of data and risk to individuals. It has extra duties.
Data Protection Board of India
The body that deals with complaints, inquiries and penalties.

b.x: 34.3 Key obligations in simple words

x: Notice and consent: personal data is mainly processed on free, specific, informed, unconditional and unambiguous consent for a stated purpose, after a clear notice. Withdrawing consent must be as easy as giving it. The Act also lists certain legitimate uses where consent is not needed, such as some State functions and medical emergencies.
Purpose limitation and data minimisation: process only what the stated purpose needs.
Accuracy and completeness: keep data reasonably accurate when it is used to take decisions about the person.

Reasonable security safeguards: protect data and prevent breaches. The Rules give examples such as encryption, obfuscation, masking, virtual tokens, access control, monitoring and logging, and measures to keep data available and intact.

Breach intimation: inform the Board and each affected Data Principal. Under the Rules the Board is informed without delay, followed by a detailed report within 72 hours (the Board can extend it on written request), and affected persons are informed without delay.

Retention and erasure: erase data when the purpose is over or consent is withdrawn, unless law requires retention. Under the Rules, personal data, traffic data and certain logs are to be retained for at least one year for specified purposes, and some large e-commerce, social media and online gaming platforms must erase data after three years of inactivity, after giving 48 hours' notice.

Children: verifiable parental consent is needed for anyone under 18, and tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children are restricted, with limited exemptions for areas such as healthcare and education.

Significant Data Fiduciaries: appoint a Data Protection Officer based in India and an independent auditor, perform periodic Data Protection Impact Assessments and audits, and follow additional due-diligence rules.
Grievance redressal: publish contact details and respond to complaints.

b.x: 34.4 Rights of a Data Principal

x: Right to access information about the personal data being processed and the parties with whom it has been shared.
Right to correction, completion and updating of personal data.
Right to erasure of personal data that is no longer needed for its purpose.
Right to grievance redressal.
Right to nominate another person to exercise rights in case of death or incapacity.

b.x: Data Principals also have duties, for example not to file false or frivolous complaints.
34.5 Penalties

The Act has a schedule of monetary penalties imposed by the Data Protection Board after an inquiry. The highest amounts are up to ₹250 crore for failing to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a personal data breach, and up to ₹200 crore for failing to notify the Board and affected persons of a breach or for breaching the children's data obligations. Smaller maximum amounts apply to other breaches of duty. These are maximums, not fixed fines, and the Board considers factors such as the nature, gravity and duration of the breach. Check the current text of the Act for the exact schedule.
34.6 Timeline of commencement (phased)

x: 13 November 2025
Rules notified. Provisions on definitions, setting up the Data Protection Board and its procedures, and rule-making powers come into force immediately.
13 November 2026
Rule 4 on registration and obligations of Consent Managers takes effect (one year after notification).

Core obligations take effect (18 months after notification): notice and consent, security safeguards, breach intimation, retention, children's data, SDF duties, rights of Data Principals and cross-border transfer rules.
Until then
Section 43A of the IT Act, 2000 and the SPDI Rules, 2011 remain in force.

b.x: 34.7 Mapping the law to database design
Compliance becomes easier when the schema is designed for it from the start. Typical patterns are shown below.

x: -- Consent is recorded per person, per purpose, with evidence
CREATE TABLE consent (
consent_id     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
principal_id   INTEGER NOT NULL,
purpose        TEXT NOT NULL,      -- e.g. 'order_updates'
notice_version TEXT NOT NULL,      -- which notice text was shown
given_at       TEXT NOT NULL,
withdrawn_at   TEXT,               -- NULL while active
channel        TEXT                -- app, web, consent manager
-- Every personal-data column has a purpose and a retention rule
CREATE TABLE data_catalog (
table_name TEXT, column_name TEXT,
purpose TEXT, retention_days INTEGER,
is_sensitive INTEGER DEFAULT 0);
-- Scheduled retention job (SQLite-style date function)
DELETE FROM customer_activity
WHERE last_activity < date('now', '-3 years');
Purpose column or table: store why each data item was collected, so that you can refuse reuse for a different purpose.
Erasure workflow: a stored procedure or job that deletes or anonymises the person's rows across all tables, queues, caches and backups' restore processes, and records that the request was completed.
Audit logs: record who accessed which personal data and when, and keep the logs for the period the rules require. Protect logs from tampering.
Pseudonymization: keep identifiers in one protected table and use surrogate IDs elsewhere, so that most systems never see real identities.
Access control and encryption: apply the least-privilege, masking and encryption techniques studied earlier.
Breach readiness: monitoring that detects unusual exports and a runbook for reporting within the time limits.

b.x: 34.8 Other frameworks in brief

x: GDPR (European Union)

Applies to personal data of people in the EU. Lawful bases include consent, contract and legitimate interests. Rights include access, rectification, erasure, portability and objection. Breach notification to the authority is normally within 72 hours. Fines can be very large, up to a percentage of worldwide turnover.
PCI-DSS

An industry standard for organisations that store, process or transmit payment card data. It requires measures such as network segmentation, strong access control, encryption of stored card data and logging.
HIPAA (United States)
Protects health information handled by covered healthcare entities and their business associates, with privacy and security rules for such data.

Do not assume that every database needs 'consent' for every row. The Act recognises some legitimate uses without consent. Also do not assume that deleting a row from the live table is enough if copies stay in caches, exports and analytics tables.

Remember the three roles (Data Principal, Data Fiduciary, Data Processor), the idea of phased commencement with the final big date of 13 May 2027, and at least three database design consequences: consent records, retention jobs and audit logs.

sec.t: NoSQL Data Models Compared: Key-Value, Document, Wide-Column, Graph, Time-Series and Search
sec.s: The six NoSQL families, Redis data structures and persistence, and how to choose a model for a problem.

b.x: 35.1 Why so many NoSQL models?

Section 14 introduced the contrast between SQL and NoSQL. 'NoSQL' is not one technology but a group of data models, each built for a particular shape of data and a particular access pattern. Choosing the right family is more important than choosing a brand name.

x: Family
Data model, examples and best use
Key-value
A giant dictionary: key to opaque value. Examples: Redis, Amazon DynamoDB (also document-like), Riak. Best for caching, sessions, counters and shopping carts.
Document
JSON-like documents grouped in collections, with indexes on fields. Examples: MongoDB, Couchbase, Firestore. Best for catalogues, content, user profiles.
Wide-column
Rows addressed by partition key with flexible columns and clustering order. Examples: Cassandra, HBase, ScyllaDB. Best for huge write-heavy data such as logs, messages and telemetry.
Graph
Nodes and relationships with properties. Examples: Neo4j, Amazon Neptune. Best for social networks, fraud rings, recommendations.
Time-series
Timestamped measurements with compression, retention and down-sampling. Examples: InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus. Best for metrics, sensors and monitoring.
Search
Inverted indexes over text. Examples: Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Apache Solr. Best for full-text search, log analysis and autocomplete.
Family
Main strength and main weakness
Key-value
Very fast and simple; weak queries, because you usually can search only by key.
Document
Flexible schema and natural fit with application objects; joins and multi-document consistency need more care.
Wide-column
Scales writes across many nodes; query patterns must be designed in advance and ad hoc queries are poor.
Graph
Fast multi-hop traversal; not designed for bulk analytics over all data or for simple tabular reports.
Time-series
Efficient storage and range queries on time; narrow focus.
Search
Relevance ranking and fuzzy matching; usually not the primary source of truth, since it favours speed of search over strict consistency.

b.x: 35.2 Key-value stores and Redis

A key-value store is the simplest database: put(key, value) and get(key). Redis is an in-memory data structure server. Besides plain strings it provides richer value types, each with its own commands.

x: String
Text, number or bytes. Commands: SET, GET, INCR, EXPIRE.
Hash
A small map of fields and values, good for objects. HSET, HGET, HGETALL.
List
Ordered list. LPUSH, RPUSH, LPOP, LRANGE. Used for queues.
Set
Unique unordered items. SADD, SMEMBERS, SINTER. Used for tags and unique visitors.
Sorted set
Unique members with a numeric score kept in order. ZADD, ZRANGE, ZREVRANGE. Used for leaderboards.
-- redis-cli examples
SET session:42 "user=aarav" EX 1800     # expires in 30 minutes
GET session:42
INCR page:views:home                      # atomic counter
HSET user:1 name Meera course BCA
HGETALL user:1
ZADD leaderboard 950 aarav 870 meera 910 kabir
ZREVRANGE leaderboard 0 2 WITHSCORES      # top 3
TTL session:42                            # seconds left

b.x: 35.3 TTL and persistence in Redis
A Time To Live (TTL) makes a key disappear automatically after a number of seconds, which suits sessions and caches. Because Redis keeps data in memory, it offers two main ways to survive a restart.

x: RDB snapshots
A point-in-time dump of the dataset saved at intervals. Compact and fast to load, but changes since the last snapshot can be lost after a crash.
AOF (append-only file)

Every write command is appended to a log and replayed at startup. Safer, because the fsync policy can be set to every write or every second, but the file is larger and slower to load. It is periodically rewritten to stay small.

b.x: Many deployments use both. Redis is also commonly used purely as a cache in front of a relational database, where losing the data is acceptable because it can be rebuilt. The licensing of Redis and the existence of forks have changed over recent years, so check the current terms if licensing matters to your project.
35.4 Document model in brief

A document database stores self-contained JSON or BSON documents. One document can hold an order with its items inside it, so a single read returns everything. The next section studies MongoDB, the best-known example, in depth.
35.5 Wide-column model in brief

In Cassandra a table has a partition key, which decides the node that stores the row, and optional clustering columns that decide the order of rows inside the partition. Queries must name the partition key, so tables are designed per query, and data is often duplicated on purpose. Section 16 and the storage-engine section explain more.
35.6 Time-series databases

A time-series database stores values that arrive in time order, such as CPU usage every 10 seconds or a temperature sensor reading. It is optimised for append-heavy writes, time-range queries, compression of similar neighbouring values, retention policies (delete data older than 90 days) and down-sampling (keep per-minute data for a week, but only hourly averages for a year).

x: -- PostgreSQL with the TimescaleDB extension (illustration)
SELECT create_hypertable('sensor_data', 'ts');
SELECT time_bucket('1 hour', ts) AS hour, avg(temp)
FROM sensor_data
WHERE ts > now() - interval '1 day'
GROUP BY hour ORDER BY hour;

b.x: 35.7 Search engines and the inverted index

A normal index maps a document to its words. An inverted index does the opposite: it maps each word to the list of documents that contain it. Searching for 'database security' becomes a fast lookup and intersection of two lists, and the engine can rank results using relevance scores such as TF-IDF or BM25.

x: Doc1: "database security basics"
Doc2: "database indexing"
Doc3: "network security"
database -> [Doc1, Doc2]
security -> [Doc1, Doc3]
indexing -> [Doc2]
query 'database security' -> Doc1 (in both lists)

b.x: 35.8 Polyglot persistence and how to choose

Polyglot persistence means using several databases in one system, each for what it does best. An online shop could keep orders in a relational database, product catalogue in a document store, sessions and cart in Redis, search in Elasticsearch, and recommendations in a graph database. The price is more systems to operate, secure, back up and keep in sync.

x: Write down the main access patterns: by key, by range, by text, by relationship, by time.
Decide how strong the consistency must be. Money usually needs strong consistency.
Estimate data size and growth. Does it fit on one machine?
Check whether the data shape changes often (favours flexible schemas).
Start with a relational database unless a clear need pushes you elsewhere; add specialised stores when a measured problem appears.

Choosing NoSQL because it is fashionable or 'faster'. A well-indexed relational database handles most workloads, and many NoSQL systems give up joins and transactions that the application then has to rebuild by hand.
For a question 'which database for X', name the access pattern first, then the family, then an example product and one trade-off.

sec.t: MongoDB in Depth: Modeling, Indexes, Aggregation, Transactions, Replica Sets and Sharding
sec.s: Embed versus reference, schema validation, indexes, the aggregation pipeline, ACID transactions, replica sets and shard keys.

b.x: 36.1 Thinking in documents

Section 15 introduced MongoDB. Here we go deeper. A good MongoDB design starts from the application's queries, not from entity diagrams. The basic design question is whether related data should be embedded inside one document or kept in separate collections and referenced by an identifier.
36.2 Embed or reference?

x: Embed when
The child data is always read together with the parent, belongs to one parent, and is limited in size. Example: the shipping address and line items of one order.
Reference when
The child data is large or grows without limit, is shared by many parents, or is updated independently. Example: the list of all comments on a popular blog post, or a product shared by many orders.
Rule of thumb
One-to-few: embed. One-to-many: embed or reference depending on size. One-to-squillions: reference, usually storing the parent id in the child.
Hard limit
A single BSON document can be at most 16 MB, so unbounded arrays are a design smell.
// embedded order
db.orders.insertOne({
customer: { id: 7, name: "Meera" },
items: [
{ sku: "B-12", qty: 2, price: 450 },
{ sku: "C-90", qty: 1, price: 1200 }
status: "PLACED",
created: new Date()
// referenced: items kept elsewhere
db.order_items.insertOne({ order_id: 1001, sku: "B-12", qty: 2 })
Embedding the customer's name inside the order keeps the name as it was at the time of purchase. This duplication is intentional and often exactly what a business wants for historical records.

b.x: 36.3 Schema validation
MongoDB is schema-flexible, not schema-less in practice. You can attach a JSON Schema validator to a collection so that bad documents are rejected.

x: db.createCollection("students", {
validator: { $jsonSchema: {
bsonType: "object",
required: ["name", "course"],
properties: {
name:   { bsonType: "string" },
course: { enum: ["BCA", "BBA", "BSc"] },
marks:  { bsonType: "int", minimum: 0, maximum: 100 }
validationAction: "error"

b.x: 36.4 Indexes
Without an index, a query scans the whole collection. MongoDB indexes are B-tree based. Every collection has an index on _id.

x: db.students.createIndex({ course: 1 })              // single field
db.students.createIndex({ course: 1, marks: -1 })     // compound
db.sessions.createIndex({ created: 1 },
{ expireAfterSeconds: 3600 }) // TTL index
db.articles.createIndex({ body: "text" })              // text index
db.students.find({ course: "BCA" }).explain("executionStats")

Compound index order matters: an index on (course, marks) supports queries on course alone and on course plus marks, but not on marks alone. Put equality fields first, then sort fields, then range fields.
TTL index: a background task deletes documents when the date field is older than the given number of seconds.
Text index: supports keyword search, but a dedicated search engine is better for advanced ranking.
Too many indexes slow down writes and use memory, so create only what queries need.

b.x: 36.5 The aggregation pipeline

The aggregation pipeline passes documents through a series of stages. Each stage transforms the stream, like a pipe in a shell. The common stages are $match (filter, like WHERE), $group (group and aggregate, like GROUP BY), $sort, $project (choose or compute fields), $limit and $lookup (a left outer join to another collection).

x: Collection orders has documents { customer, status, amount }.
Goal: total amount per customer for DELIVERED orders, highest first, top 2.
Sample data: (A, DELIVERED, 500) (A, DELIVERED, 300) (B, DELIVERED, 900) (B, CANCELLED, 700) (C, DELIVERED, 200)
db.orders.aggregate([
{ $match: { status: "DELIVERED" } },
{ $group: { _id: "$customer", total: { $sum: "$amount" } } },
{ $sort: { total: -1 } },
{ $limit: 2 }
// after $match : A500, A300, B900, C200
// after $group : { _id:A, total:800 } { _id:B, total:900 } { _id:C, total:200 }
// after $sort  : B900, A800, C200
// result       : { _id: "B", total: 900 }, { _id: "A", total: 800 }

b.x: The SQL equivalent is SELECT customer, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders WHERE status='DELIVERED' GROUP BY customer ORDER BY total DESC LIMIT 2. Put $match as early as possible so that later stages process fewer documents and indexes can help.

x: // join with $lookup
db.orders.aggregate([
{ $lookup: {
from: "customers",
localField: "customer",
foreignField: "_id",
as: "cust" } },
{ $unwind: "$cust" }

b.x: 36.6 Transactions

Single-document operations in MongoDB are atomic, even when the document has many embedded parts. This is one reason to model related data inside one document. Since version 4.0 MongoDB also supports multi-document ACID transactions on replica sets, and later versions extend this to sharded clusters. They are useful, for example, for transferring money between two account documents, but they cost more: they hold resources, add latency, and should be short. A schema that needs transactions everywhere is often a sign that a relational database or a better document design is needed.

x: const session = db.getMongo().startSession();
session.startTransaction();
const acc = session.getDatabase("bank").accounts;
acc.updateOne({ _id: 1 }, { $inc: { bal: -500 } });
acc.updateOne({ _id: 2 }, { $inc: { bal:  500 } });
session.commitTransaction();   // or abortTransaction()

b.x: 36.7 Replica sets

A replica set is a group of MongoDB servers holding the same data. One member is the primary and receives all writes. The other members are secondaries that copy the primary's operation log (oplog). If the primary fails, the remaining members hold an election and choose a new primary, which needs a majority of voting members. That is why replica sets normally have an odd number of voting members, such as 3. An arbiter can vote without holding data.

x: writes                 oplog\
|  PRIMARY  | ----> | SECONDARY 1 |
clients        > | SECONDARY 2 |
Primary fails -> election -> a secondary becomes primary
Write concern controls how many members must confirm a write. w: 'majority' gives stronger durability.
Read preference lets reads go to secondaries, which may return slightly old data (replication lag).
Read concern controls the isolation of reads, such as 'majority'.

b.x: 36.8 Sharding and the shard key

When one replica set is too small for the data or the traffic, MongoDB shards the collection across several replica sets. A mongos router sends each query to the right shard using the shard key, and config servers keep the cluster metadata. The shard key is the most important decision, and it is difficult to change later.

x: Ranged shard key
Neighbouring key values live together, so range queries are efficient. But a steadily increasing key such as a timestamp or ObjectId sends all new writes to the last chunk, creating a hot spot.
Hashed shard key
The key is hashed, so values spread evenly and writes are balanced. Range queries must contact many shards.
Good key
High cardinality, even distribution, matches the common query filter. A compound key such as (customer_id, order_date) is common.
sh.enableSharding("shop")
sh.shardCollection("shop.orders", { customer_id: "hashed" })
Choosing a monotonically increasing field as a ranged shard key. All inserts then go to one shard and the other shards stay idle.
Be ready to explain: embed vs reference with an example, what a replica set election is, and ranged vs hashed shard keys with the hot-spot problem.

sec.t: Graph Databases and the Cypher Query Language
sec.s: Property graph model, Cypher patterns, comparison with SQL joins and recursive queries, graph algorithms and use cases.

b.x: 37.1 Why graphs?

Many problems are really about relationships: who is a friend of a friend, which accounts share a phone number, which products do people with similar tastes buy. In a relational database each hop needs a join, and a query that goes four or five hops deep can become slow and hard to write. A graph database stores relationships directly as first-class data, so following a relationship is a quick pointer-like step from one node to its neighbours, whatever the total size of the data.
37.2 The property graph model

x: Node: an entity, such as a Person or a Product. A node can have one or more labels, such as :Person.
Relationship (edge): a directed, typed connection between two nodes, such as FOLLOWS or BOUGHT. It always has a start node, an end node and a type.
Properties: key-value pairs on nodes and on relationships, such as name: 'Aarav' or since: 2024.
(Aarav:Person)--[:FOLLOWS {since:2024}]-->(Meera:Person)
(Meera:Person)--[:FOLLOWS]-->(Kabir:Person)
(Aarav:Person)--[:LIKES]-->(Book:Product {title:'DBMS'})

b.x: 37.3 Cypher basics

Cypher is the declarative query language of Neo4j and has influenced the ISO graph query language GQL. It uses ASCII-art patterns: round brackets for nodes and square brackets with arrows for relationships.

x: // CREATE nodes and relationships
CREATE (a:Person {name:'Aarav', city:'Delhi'}),
(m:Person {name:'Meera', city:'Pune'}),
(k:Person {name:'Kabir', city:'Delhi'}),
(a)-[:FOLLOWS]->(m),
(m)-[:FOLLOWS]->(k)
// MATCH + WHERE + RETURN
MATCH (p:Person)-[:FOLLOWS]->(f:Person)
WHERE p.name = 'Aarav'
RETURN f.name, f.city
// MERGE: create only if it does not exist
MERGE (p:Person {name:'Ishita'})
// SET and DELETE
MATCH (p:Person {name:'Kabir'}) SET p.city = 'Mumbai'
MATCH (p:Person {name:'Ishita'}) DETACH DELETE p
CREATE
Always creates the pattern, even if a copy exists.
MATCH
Finds all subgraphs that fit the pattern.
MERGE
Matches the pattern or creates it when missing, so repeated runs do not duplicate data.
SET
Adds or changes properties and labels.
DELETE / DETACH DELETE
Removes nodes or relationships. A node with relationships needs DETACH DELETE.
RETURN
Chooses what is output, with aggregation such as count().

b.x: 37.4 Multi-hop, variable-length and shortest paths

x: // friends of friends of Aarav (exactly 2 hops)
MATCH (a:Person {name:'Aarav'})-[:FOLLOWS*2]->(fof)
RETURN DISTINCT fof.name
// anyone reachable within 1 to 4 hops
MATCH (a:Person {name:'Aarav'})-[:FOLLOWS*1..4]->(x)
RETURN DISTINCT x.name
// shortest path between two people
MATCH p = shortestPath(
(a:Person {name:'Aarav'})-[:FOLLOWS*]-(b:Person {name:'Kabir'}))
RETURN p, length(p)
// recommendation: people followed by those I follow, not yet by me
MATCH (me:Person {name:'Aarav'})-[:FOLLOWS]->()-[:FOLLOWS]->(rec)
WHERE NOT (me)-[:FOLLOWS]->(rec) AND rec <> me
RETURN rec.name, count(*) AS mutual ORDER BY mutual DESC

b.x: 37.5 The same question in SQL

Suppose follows(src, dst) is a relational table. 'Everybody reachable from Aarav' needs a recursive common table expression. The following works in SQLite (3.8.3 and later), PostgreSQL and MySQL 8, with small differences in syntax.

x: WITH RECURSIVE reach(person, depth) AS (
SELECT dst, 1 FROM follows WHERE src = 'Aarav'
UNION
SELECT f.dst, r.depth + 1
FROM follows f JOIN reach r ON f.src = r.person
WHERE r.depth < 4
SELECT DISTINCT person FROM reach;

b.x: It works, but the query is longer, harder to read and, on a large table, each level performs a join with the full follows table, unless it is well indexed. A graph database avoids this by storing, for each node, direct references to its relationships. This is called index-free adjacency in some systems. The result is that traversal cost depends on the part of the graph that is touched, not on the total number of relationships.
37.6 Graph algorithms

x: Shortest path: the fewest hops (or lowest total weight) between two nodes, used in routing and 'degrees of separation'.
PageRank: scores a node by the number and importance of nodes that link to it. Originally used to rank web pages.
Community detection: finds groups of densely connected nodes, such as friend circles or fraud rings.
Centrality (degree, betweenness): finds influential or bridge nodes.
Similarity: finds nodes with similar neighbours, which supports recommendations.

b.x: 37.7 Typical use cases

x: Fraud detection: several accounts sharing the same device, phone number and address form a suspicious cluster.
Recommendation: customers who bought X also bought Y, found through shared purchases.
Knowledge graphs: facts linked as entities and relationships, used in search and AI assistants.
Network and IT operations: dependency graphs, impact analysis of a server failure.
Identity and access management: users, groups, roles and permissions form a graph.

b.x: 37.8 RDF and SPARQL in brief

A different graph model, RDF, stores facts as triples: subject, predicate, object, such as (Aarav, follows, Meera). Queries are written in SPARQL. RDF is common in the semantic web and linked open data, while the property graph is more common in application development.

x: Using a graph database for tabular reports or heavy aggregations over all rows. Graphs shine when queries start at a few nodes and walk outward. A relational or columnar system is usually better for whole-table analysis.
State the three parts of the property graph (nodes, relationships, properties), give one Cypher MATCH example, and explain why multi-hop queries are easier than SQL joins.

sec.t: Distributed Database Fundamentals: Sharding, Replication, Consistency Models and Consensus
sec.s: How data is split and copied across machines, how consistency is traded for speed, and how nodes agree.

b.x: 38.1 Why distribute a database?

A single machine has limits in storage, throughput and availability. Distributing data across several machines gives scalability (more data and more requests), availability (service continues when a node fails) and lower latency (data near users). The price is complexity: network failures, partial failures and the difficulty of keeping copies consistent. Topic 18 of the base notes introduced the CAP theorem; this topic builds the mechanisms.
38.2 Partitioning (sharding)

Vertical partitioning splits a table by columns (rarely accessed large columns go elsewhere). Horizontal partitioning, called sharding when the parts live on different machines, splits a table by rows. Each shard holds a subset of the rows.

x: Range sharding
Rows are assigned by key ranges (A to F, G to M, ...). Range queries are efficient, but hot spots appear if keys grow in order, such as timestamps: the newest range receives all inserts.
Hash sharding
shard = hash(key) mod N. Spreads load evenly, but range queries touch every shard, and changing N moves almost every key.
Directory-based sharding
A lookup table maps each key (or key range) to a shard. Very flexible but the directory is a bottleneck and a single point of failure unless replicated.

b.x: 38.3 Consistent hashing

Plain hash mod N reshuffles nearly all data when a node is added or removed. Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a circular hash space (a ring). A key belongs to the first node found clockwise from the key's position. When a node joins or leaves, only the keys between it and its neighbour move.

x: Ring positions 0..99.   Nodes:  A at 10,  B at 40,  C at 75
key position :   5    25    50    80    95
owner        :   A     B     C     A     A     (next node clockwise)
Add node D at 60. Only keys in (40, 60] move from C to D:
owner        :   A     B     D     A     A      (only key 50 moved)

b.x: Real systems give each physical node many virtual nodes (points on the ring) so that load is balanced and a failed node's data is spread over many others. Dynamo-style systems such as Cassandra use this idea.
38.4 Replication topologies

x: Single-leader (primary-replica)
All writes go to one leader, which streams changes to followers. Reads can use followers. Simple, no write conflicts; the leader is a bottleneck and a failure needs a failover.
Multi-leader
Several nodes accept writes (for example one per data centre) and exchange changes. Good for multi-region writes; needs conflict resolution when the same row is changed in two places.
Leaderless
Any replica accepts writes; the client or a coordinator sends each write to several replicas and reads from several. Used by Dynamo, Cassandra and Riak; relies on quorums.

b.x: Replication lag: an asynchronous follower can be behind the leader, so a user may not see their own write (read-your-writes violation) or may see time go backwards. Remedies include reading from the leader after a write, session guarantees, or synchronous replication to at least one follower.
38.5 Quorums

With N replicas of each item, a write must be acknowledged by W replicas and a read must contact R replicas. If R + W > N, every read set overlaps every write set in at least one replica, so a read sees the latest acknowledged write (provided the system picks the newest version).

x: N = 3,  W = 2,  R = 2   R + W = 4 > 3   read always overlaps the latest write
N = 3,  W = 3,  R = 1   R + W = 4 > 3   fast reads, writes need all replicas
N = 3,  W = 1,  R = 1   R + W = 2 < 3   fast but reads may be stale (eventual)
N = 5,  W = 3,  R = 3   R + W = 6 > 5   tolerates 2 failed replicas

b.x: Quorums reduce, but do not completely remove, anomalies: concurrent writes, sloppy quorums and failed writes can still produce surprises, so systems add the following repair mechanisms.

x: Read repair: when a read finds a replica with an old version, the coordinator writes the newest version back to it.
Hinted handoff: if a replica is down, another node stores the write as a hint and delivers it when the replica returns.
Anti-entropy: background comparison of replicas, often with Merkle trees, to find and fix differences.

b.x: 38.6 Ordering versions: timestamps and vector clocks

Last-write-wins (LWW) keeps the version with the highest timestamp; it is simple but loses concurrent updates and depends on synchronised clocks. A vector clock keeps one counter per node with each version. If one version's vector is greater than or equal to another's in every position, it is the newer one; if neither dominates, the versions are concurrent and the application (or a merge rule) must reconcile them. Conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs), such as counters and sets, are designed so that concurrent updates merge automatically without conflicts.
38.7 Consistency models

x: Linearizable (strong)
Every operation appears to take effect instantly at some point between its start and end; all clients see the same order. Looks like a single copy. Highest cost in latency.
Sequential
All clients see the same order of operations, but it need not match real time.
Causal
Operations that are causally related are seen in order by everyone; unrelated ones may be seen in different orders.
Eventual
If no new updates occur, all replicas eventually converge. No guarantee about what a read returns meanwhile.

b.x: 38.8 ACID versus BASE

Relational systems promise ACID. Many distributed NoSQL systems follow BASE: Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent. BASE trades immediate consistency for availability and speed. The two are ends of a spectrum, and many modern systems let you choose per operation.
38.9 CAP and PACELC

CAP says that when a network partition occurs a distributed system must choose between consistency and availability (partition tolerance is not optional in a real network). It says nothing about normal operation. Daniel Abadi's PACELC theorem completes the picture: if there is a Partition, choose between Availability and Consistency; Else (normal operation), choose between Latency and Consistency. Even without failures, waiting for replicas to agree costs latency.

x: PA/EL
Prefer availability under partition and low latency otherwise. Typical of Dynamo-style and Cassandra defaults (tunable).
PC/EC
Prefer consistency in both cases. Typical of strongly consistent systems such as HBase or traditional relational clusters with synchronous replication.
PA/EC
Available under partition but consistent otherwise. Some MongoDB configurations are described this way.
PC/EL
Consistent under partition but low latency otherwise. PNUTS is the usual example.
Real products are configurable (quorum sizes, read concerns), so the placement of a product in PACELC depends on its settings. Treat the table as typical defaults, not fixed labels.

b.x: 38.10 Consensus: Paxos and Raft

To keep several nodes in agreement (on a leader, on the order of log entries, on commit), distributed systems use consensus algorithms. Paxos is the classic, famous for being hard to understand. Raft was designed to be understandable and is used in etcd, Consul, CockroachDB and others.

x: Leader election: nodes start as followers; if a follower hears nothing from a leader for a randomized timeout, it becomes a candidate, increases the term number and asks for votes. A candidate with votes from a majority becomes leader.
Log replication: the leader appends client commands to its log and sends them to followers. An entry is committed when a majority of nodes has stored it; then it is applied to the state machine.
Majority rule: with 2f + 1 nodes the system tolerates f failures. Three nodes tolerate one failure, five tolerate two.
Safety: a node can win an election only if its log is up to date, so committed entries are never lost.

Treating CAP as 'pick any two'. Partition tolerance is not optional; the real choice during a partition is consistency or availability, and during normal operation it is latency or consistency (PACELC).
Quorum rule R + W > N, the three replication topologies, consistent hashing's advantage (few keys move), and PACELC's four classes are the standard exam items for this topic.

sec.t: Storage Engines: B-Tree vs LSM-Tree, Column Stores and In-Memory Databases
sec.s: How data is laid out on disk and in memory, and why write-heavy, read-heavy and analytic systems choose different engines.

b.x: 39.1 What is a storage engine?

The storage engine is the part of a database that stores, finds and updates data on disk or in memory. The same SQL layer can sit above different engines (MySQL has InnoDB and others; MongoDB has WiredTiger). The engine's data structure decides whether the system is fast at reads, at writes or at scans over huge tables.
39.2 The write-ahead log

Almost every engine first appends each change to a sequential write-ahead log (WAL) so that it can recover after a crash (Unit 3, ARIES). Sequential appends are much faster than random page writes, a fact that LSM-trees exploit even further.
39.3 B-tree engines

A B-tree (really a B+ tree in most systems, Topic 18) keeps data in sorted order in fixed-size pages and updates pages in place. A read follows a few page pointers. A write finds the page, modifies it and may split it. Strengths: predictable read latency, excellent range scans, mature concurrency control. Weaknesses: random I/O for writes, write amplification (a one-row change rewrites a whole page plus the WAL entry) and page fragmentation.
39.4 LSM-tree engines
A log-structured merge tree (LSM-tree) turns random writes into sequential ones.

x: Writes go to the WAL and into an in-memory sorted structure called the memtable.
When the memtable is full it is written to disk as an immutable sorted file, an SSTable (sorted string table).
Reads check the memtable first, then SSTables from newest to oldest. A Bloom filter per SSTable tells quickly whether a key is definitely not in that file, saving disk reads.
Background compaction merges SSTables, discarding overwritten and deleted values (deletes are written as tombstones) and keeping the number of files small.
write -> WAL (sequential) + memtable (RAM)
v  flush when full
Level 0:  [SST] [SST] [SST]        newest
\  |  /   compaction
Level 1:     [ bigger SST files ]
Level 2:   [ even bigger, sorted, non-overlapping ]   oldest
read -> memtable -> Bloom filter + SSTables (newest first)

b.x: LSM-trees give very high write throughput and good compression, which is why Cassandra, RocksDB, LevelDB and HBase use them. The cost is that reads may need to look in several files, and compaction uses CPU and disk bandwidth in the background.
39.5 Comparing B-tree and LSM-tree

x: Write path
B-tree: random in-place page writes. LSM: sequential appends and flushes.
Read path
B-tree: one search through the tree. LSM: memtable plus possibly several SSTables, softened by Bloom filters.
Write amplification
B-tree: a page rewrite per change. LSM: data is rewritten several times during compaction; the amount depends on the strategy.
Read amplification
Higher for LSM (several files), lower for B-tree.
Space amplification
LSM holds old versions until compaction; B-trees waste space in half-empty pages.
Range scans
Excellent in both when files are well compacted; B-tree is more predictable.
Best for
B-tree: balanced read-heavy OLTP. LSM: write-heavy ingestion, time-series, logs.

b.x: 39.6 Row stores and column stores

A row store keeps all attributes of a row together, which is ideal when a query needs most of a row (OLTP: fetch or update one customer). A column store keeps each column's values together. An analytic query such as SUM(amount) over a billion rows reads only the amount column, not the other columns, saving most of the I/O.

x: Row store (pages):       [1, Asha, CSE, 8.6] [2, Ravi, ECE, 7.2] ...
Column store (files):    id:   1 2 3 ...
name: Asha Ravi Meera ...
dept: CSE ECE CSE ...   (repeated values compress well)
Compression: values in one column are similar and often repeated, so techniques such as run-length encoding, dictionary encoding and bit-packing give large savings.
Vectorized execution: operators process batches of thousands of values at a time, using CPU caches and SIMD instructions efficiently.

Weak at single-row inserts and updates (a row is spread over many column files), so column stores load data in batches. Examples include ClickHouse, Apache Parquet files for data lakes, and the column-store engines in warehouse products.
Some systems combine both: row format for recent data, column format for older data (hybrid or HTAP designs).

b.x: 39.7 In-memory databases

An in-memory database keeps the working data in RAM, removing disk reads and allowing data structures optimized for memory. Examples: Redis, Memcached (caching), SAP HANA and VoltDB. Durability is handled by periodic snapshots (writing the whole state to disk), by an append-only command log, or by replication to other nodes. Costs: RAM is expensive and limited, and a crash may lose the most recent changes unless the log is synchronous.
39.8 Choosing an engine

x: Balanced OLTP with many reads
B-tree engine (InnoDB, PostgreSQL heap with B-tree indexes).
Heavy write ingestion, time series, event logs
LSM engine (Cassandra, RocksDB-based systems).
Analytics over big tables
Column store with compression and vectorized execution.
Sub-millisecond lookups, caches, leaderboards
In-memory store (Redis) with an appropriate persistence mode.

Give the LSM write path in four words: WAL, memtable, SSTable, compaction. For comparison say B-trees optimise reads and in-place updates, LSM-trees optimise write throughput at the cost of read and compaction work.

sec.t: NewSQL, Distributed SQL and Cloud Databases
sec.s: Systems that combine SQL and ACID transactions with horizontal scale, and the cloud services that run databases for you.

b.x: 40.1 The problem NewSQL tries to solve

Relational databases give SQL and ACID transactions, but traditionally scale up (a bigger machine) rather than out. NoSQL systems scale out but gave up joins, SQL and strong consistency. NewSQL (distributed SQL) systems aim for both: a SQL interface with ACID transactions over data that is automatically partitioned and replicated across many nodes.
40.2 Typical architecture

x: Data is divided into small ranges or partitions, each replicated on several nodes.
Each range uses a consensus protocol (Raft or Paxos, Topic 38) to keep its replicas consistent and to elect a leader.

Transactions that touch several ranges use a distributed commit protocol, close to two-phase commit built on top of the consensus groups (Unit 3, Topic 39), combined with multiversion concurrency control.
A SQL layer parses and plans queries, and sends work to the nodes that hold the data, often pushing filters and aggregates down to them.
Nodes can be added or removed and ranges rebalanced automatically.

b.x: 40.3 Google Spanner and TrueTime

Google Spanner is the system that popularised the idea. It offers externally consistent (linearizable) distributed transactions across data centres around the world. Its key idea is TrueTime, an API that exposes the uncertainty of the clock as an interval using GPS receivers and atomic clocks. A transaction chooses a commit timestamp and then waits until it is sure the timestamp is in the past everywhere ('commit wait'), so that timestamps agree with real-time order.
40.4 Examples of distributed SQL systems

x: Google Spanner
Managed service; strongly consistent global SQL; the model for others.
CockroachDB
PostgreSQL-compatible wire protocol and SQL, Raft-based replication of ranges, serializable transactions by default.
TiDB
MySQL-compatible SQL layer over a distributed key-value store (TiKV) using Raft; separate columnar storage for analytic queries, so it markets itself as HTAP.
YugabyteDB
PostgreSQL-compatible SQL layer over a distributed document store with Raft replication.
Product features and licences change quickly (several of these moved to different licence models in recent years), so always check the current documentation before choosing one.

b.x: 40.5 HTAP

Hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP) tries to run OLTP and analytics on the same data without exporting it to a warehouse. Typical designs keep a row store for transactions and a column store replica for analytics, synchronized by the replication log. It removes ETL delay but needs careful resource isolation so that big queries do not slow transactions.
40.6 Database as a service (DBaaS)

A cloud provider runs the database for you: provisioning, patching, backups, replication and failover are automatic. Examples: Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL and AlloyDB, Azure SQL, MongoDB Atlas, managed PostgreSQL offerings. You choose the instance size and pay for use.

x: Benefits
Less administration, automatic backups and point-in-time recovery, easy replicas and failover, elastic scaling.
Costs and risks

Ongoing fees (storage, I/O, data transfer out), less control over the OS and configuration, vendor lock-in through proprietary features, shared-responsibility security (you still configure access and encryption).

b.x: 40.7 Serverless and cloud-native designs

Cloud-native databases separate compute from storage. Aurora, for example, replaces the local storage engine with a distributed storage service that replicates log records across availability zones, so replicas can be added quickly. Serverless databases scale compute up and down automatically, even to zero, and charge by usage, which suits spiky or small workloads; the trade-offs are cold start delays and less predictable cost for heavy steady loads.
40.8 Multi-region and multi-model

x: Multi-region deployments place replicas close to users and survive a region failure. Strong consistency across regions costs latency; many systems therefore let you choose per table or per query (for example follower reads at a slight staleness).

Multi-model databases support several data models (relational, document, graph, key-value) in one engine, reducing the number of systems to run; the depth of each model may be less than in a dedicated system.
Polyglot persistence uses several specialized databases in one application: a relational database for orders, Redis for sessions, a search engine for text, a graph database for relationships.

b.x: 40.9 Choosing

x: A single PostgreSQL or MySQL server (with replicas) is enough for most applications; do not distribute early.
Choose distributed SQL when you need horizontal write scaling or multi-region consistency and want to keep SQL and transactions.
Choose NoSQL when the access pattern is simple and scale or flexibility dominates.
Weigh operational cost and skills, not only features.

Assuming NewSQL removes trade-offs. Cross-node transactions still cost extra network round trips, so latency is higher than on a single node, and schema design (for example choosing keys that keep related rows together) still matters.
Define NewSQL as SQL plus ACID plus horizontal scalability. Mention consensus replication, distributed transactions and one example (Spanner or CockroachDB).

sec.s: Designing databases for analysis: star schemas, dimensions, slowly changing data, ETL, OLAP operations, lakehouses and data mining basics.

b.x: 41.1 OLTP versus OLAP

x: Purpose
OLTP: run the business (orders, payments). OLAP: analyse the business (trends, reports).
Queries
OLTP: short reads and writes of a few rows. OLAP: long scans and aggregations over millions of rows.
Data
OLTP: current, detailed, normalized. OLAP: historical, integrated, often summarized and denormalized.
Users
OLTP: many clerks and applications. OLAP: fewer analysts and managers.
Design
OLTP: normalized (3NF/BCNF) for consistency. OLAP: star or snowflake schema for read speed.
Updates
OLTP: constant. OLAP: periodic batch loads, otherwise read-only.

b.x: 41.2 What is a data warehouse?

A data warehouse is a central repository that integrates data from many operational sources and supports decision making. Inmon's classic definition lists four properties: subject-oriented (organised around subjects such as sales or customers, not applications), integrated (data from different sources is made consistent in names, formats and codes), time-variant (it keeps history, so you can compare years) and non-volatile (data is added, not changed or deleted in place).
41.3 Star schema

The standard design has a central fact table holding the measurable events (a sale: quantity, amount) with foreign keys to dimension tables that describe the context (when, what, where). The picture looks like a star. The grain of the fact table is the level of detail of one row, here 'one product in one store on one day'. Declaring the grain first prevents mistakes.

x: dim_date                dim_product
+---- fact_sales ---+
dim_store
fact_sales(date_id, product_id, store_id, qty, amount)   <- measures

b.x: Here is a small star schema with data that you can run in SQLite or in the DBMS Lab.

x: CREATE TABLE dim_date(date_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, day TEXT, month TEXT, quarter TEXT, year INT);
CREATE TABLE dim_product(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT, category TEXT);
CREATE TABLE dim_store(store_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, city TEXT, state TEXT);
CREATE TABLE fact_sales(date_id INT, product_id INT, store_id INT, qty INT, amount INT);
INSERT INTO dim_product VALUES (1,'Pen','Stationery'),(2,'Notebook','Stationery'),(3,'Bag','Accessories');
INSERT INTO dim_store VALUES (1,'Patna','Bihar'),(2,'Ranchi','Jharkhand');
-- total sales by quarter and product category
SELECT d.quarter, p.category, SUM(f.amount) AS total
FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id)
JOIN dim_product p USING (product_id)
GROUP BY d.quarter, p.category ORDER BY d.quarter, p.category;
quarter | category    | total
Q1      | Accessories | 800
Q1      | Stationery  | 550
Q2      | Accessories | 400
Q2      | Stationery  | 200
Fact tables are tall and narrow (many rows, few columns); dimension tables are short and wide (few rows, many descriptive columns).
Dimension tables use surrogate keys (meaningless integers) rather than source-system keys, so history and source changes do not break the warehouse.
Queries join the fact table to a few dimensions and aggregate: simple and fast.

b.x: 41.4 Snowflake and galaxy schemas

x: Snowflake schema
Dimensions are normalized into sub-dimensions (product to category to department). Saves space and avoids redundancy, but needs more joins and is harder to read.
Galaxy (fact constellation)
Several fact tables share dimension tables (sales and shipments both use dim_date and dim_product). Used for enterprise warehouses with several business processes.

b.x: 41.5 Slowly changing dimensions (SCD)
Dimension attributes change over time: a customer moves city, a product changes category. The SCD types say how to record such changes.

x: Type 0
Never changes (fixed attributes such as date of birth).
Type 1
Overwrite the old value. No history; reports for the past change retroactively.
Type 2
Add a new row with a new surrogate key and validity dates. Full history; the most common choice for important attributes.
Type 3
Keep the previous value in an extra column (city, previous_city). Limited history of one change.
SCD Type 2: customer Asha moves from Patna to Delhi on 2026-06-01
cust_key | cust_id | name | city  | valid_from | valid_to   | current
Sales before June point to key 101 (Patna); later sales point to key 205.

b.x: 41.6 ETL and ELT
