ETL stands for Extract, Transform, Load: data is extracted from source systems, transformed (cleaned, converted, deduplicated, integrated) in a staging area, and loaded into the warehouse. ELT loads the raw data first and transforms it inside the powerful warehouse or lake using SQL. ELT dominates in cloud platforms because storage is cheap and the warehouse engine scales.

x: Extract: full or incremental (changed rows only, using timestamps or change data capture from the log).
Transform: standardise formats, resolve duplicates, handle missing values, derive keys, apply business rules.
Load: append to fact tables, apply SCD logic to dimensions, update indexes and aggregates.

b.x: 41.7 OLAP operations and the data cube
OLAP (online analytical processing) views data as a multidimensional cube whose axes are dimensions (time, product, store) and whose cells hold measures (amount).

x: Roll-up
Aggregate to a higher level of a hierarchy: month to quarter to year.
Drill-down
The reverse: go from year to quarter to month for more detail.
Slice
Fix one dimension to a single value (quarter = Q1), giving a sub-cube.
Dice
Select a sub-cube by conditions on several dimensions.
Pivot (rotate)
Swap axes to view the data from another angle.
-- slice: Q1 only
SELECT p.category, SUM(f.amount) FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id) JOIN dim_product p USING (product_id)
WHERE d.quarter = 'Q1' GROUP BY p.category;
-- Accessories 800 | Stationery 550

b.x: SQL provides GROUP BY ROLLUP and CUBE in PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server and MySQL (ROLLUP) to compute subtotals and the grand total in one statement. SQLite has neither, but the same result is built with UNION ALL:

x: SELECT d.quarter, p.category, SUM(f.amount) FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id) JOIN dim_product p USING (product_id)
GROUP BY d.quarter, p.category
UNION ALL SELECT d.quarter, NULL, SUM(f.amount) FROM fact_sales f
JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id) GROUP BY d.quarter
UNION ALL SELECT NULL, NULL, SUM(amount) FROM fact_sales
ORDER BY 1, 2;
NULL | NULL        | 1950     <- grand total
Q1   | NULL        | 1350     <- quarter subtotal
Q1   | Accessories | 800
Q1   | Stationery  | 550
Q2   | NULL        | 600
Q2   | Accessories | 400
Q2   | Stationery  | 200

b.x: Storage styles: ROLAP uses relational tables (star schemas), MOLAP uses specialised multidimensional arrays, HOLAP combines the two. A data mart is a smaller, subject-specific warehouse (for example for sales only).
41.8 Data lake, warehouse and lakehouse

x: Data warehouse
Structured, modelled, cleaned data (schema on write). Fast SQL analytics. Higher cost per byte.
Data lake
Raw data of any format (files, logs, images) in cheap object storage (schema on read). Flexible, but without management it becomes a 'data swamp'.
Lakehouse
Adds a table layer with ACID transactions, schema enforcement and time travel on top of lake files. Open table formats include Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg and Apache Hudi.

b.x: A common organisation is the medallion architecture: bronze tables hold raw ingested data, silver tables hold cleaned and conformed data, and gold tables hold business-level aggregates for reports.
41.9 Data mining in brief

Data mining finds patterns in large data sets. The main tasks are association rules (which items occur together), classification (predict a category, such as 'will this customer churn'), clustering (group similar records without labels) and anomaly detection.

x: Five baskets: {pen, notebook}, {pen, notebook, bag}, {pen, bag}, {notebook, bag}, {pen, notebook}.
support(pen and notebook) = 3 baskets / 5 = 0.6
support(pen) = 4/5 = 0.8; support(notebook) = 4/5 = 0.8
confidence(pen → notebook) = support(pen and notebook) / support(pen) = 0.6 / 0.8 = 0.75
lift = 0.6 / (0.8 x 0.8) = 0.9375, slightly below 1, so buying a pen does not make a notebook more likely than usual.
Calling a high-confidence rule interesting without checking lift. If an item is bought by almost everyone, nearly every rule that ends with it has high confidence.
Be ready to draw a star schema, define fact and dimension, name the four OLAP operations, compare OLTP and OLAP in a table and explain ETL in three words: extract, transform, load.

sec.t: Big Data Processing in Depth: HDFS, MapReduce, Spark and Streaming with Kafka
sec.s: Storing and processing data too large for one machine, in batches and as streams.

b.x: 42.1 The idea: move computation to the data

When data is terabytes or petabytes, copying it to one powerful server is impossible. Big data systems spread the data over many ordinary machines and send small programs to where the data lives (data locality). They also assume that machines fail all the time, so every part is replicated and every task can be rerun.
42.2 HDFS: the Hadoop Distributed File System

x: Files are split into large blocks (128 MB is the common default) and each block is stored on several machines. The default replication factor is 3.
The NameNode keeps the metadata: the directory tree and which DataNodes hold which blocks. DataNodes store the blocks and send periodic heartbeats and block reports to the NameNode.
If a DataNode stops sending heartbeats, the NameNode notices and instructs other nodes to re-create the missing replicas.
HDFS is designed for large sequential reads and appends, not for many small files or low-latency random access. Files are written once and read many times.
The NameNode is a single point of failure unless a standby NameNode is configured (high availability).
File of 400 MB, block size 128 MB, replication 3
-> 4 blocks (128 + 128 + 128 + 16 MB), 12 stored block copies
NameNode:  file.csv -> [b1, b2, b3, b4]
b1 -> DN2, DN5, DN7    b2 -> DN1, DN3, DN5   ...

b.x: 42.3 MapReduce

MapReduce is a programming model for batch processing. The programmer writes two functions. map reads a record and emits key-value pairs; reduce receives one key with all its values and emits a result. Between them the framework shuffles and sorts: it groups all values of the same key and delivers them to the same reducer.

x: Input documents: D1 = 'to be or not to be', D2 = 'to do is to be'.
Map (one call per document) emits (word, 1): (to,1) (be,1) (or,1) (not,1) (to,1) (be,1) (to,1) (do,1) (is,1) (to,1) (be,1).
Shuffle and sort groups by key: to: [1,1,1,1]  be: [1,1,1]  or: [1]  not: [1]  do: [1]  is: [1].
Reduce sums each list: to = 4, be = 3, or = 1, not = 1, do = 1, is = 1.
A combiner can pre-add counts on each mapper to reduce the data sent across the network.
Fault tolerance: if a map or reduce task fails, the framework simply reruns it on another node, since the input is replicated and tasks are deterministic.
Limitation: each MapReduce job reads from and writes to disk, so iterative algorithms (machine learning, graph processing) are slow.

b.x: 42.4 Apache Spark

Spark keeps data in memory between steps, which makes iterative and interactive work much faster than disk-based MapReduce. Its core abstraction is the resilient distributed dataset (RDD), an immutable collection split into partitions across the cluster; the higher-level DataFrame API adds named columns and lets the Catalyst optimizer plan queries, much like a SQL optimizer.

x: Transformations (map, filter, join, groupBy) are lazy: they only build a plan (a lineage graph). Actions (count, collect, write) trigger the computation.
Fault tolerance through lineage: a lost partition is recomputed from the steps that produced it, without replicating intermediate data.
Spark SQL, streaming, machine learning and graph libraries share one engine.
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F      # PySpark
spark = SparkSession.builder.appName('wc').getOrCreate()
lines = spark.read.text('docs.txt')
words = lines.select(F.explode(F.split('value', ' ')).alias('word'))
counts = words.groupBy('word').count().orderBy(F.desc('count'))
counts.show()                      # action: runs the whole plan
sales = spark.read.parquet('sales/')
sales.groupBy('category').agg(F.sum('amount').alias('total')).show()

b.x: 42.5 Stream processing with Apache Kafka

Batch jobs process data that has already been collected. Streaming handles events continuously as they arrive (payments, clicks, sensor readings). Kafka is a distributed, replicated log used as the backbone for event streams.

x: Topic
A named stream of events, like a table name for events.
Partition

A topic is split into partitions; each partition is an ordered, append-only log. Ordering is guaranteed only within a partition, so events with the same key (for example the same user) go to the same partition.
Offset
The position of an event within a partition. Consumers remember their offset and can replay old events by resetting it.
Producer / consumer
Producers append events; consumers read them.
Consumer group
Consumers in a group share the partitions of a topic, each partition read by exactly one member of the group, so work is parallel and scalable. Different groups each receive all events independently.
Replication
Each partition has a leader and followers on other brokers; if the leader fails a follower takes over.
Topic 'orders' with 3 partitions, consumer group 'billing' with 3 consumers
partition 0 -> consumer A    (offsets 0,1,2,3 ...)
partition 1 -> consumer B
partition 2 -> consumer C
Another group 'analytics' reads the same events independently.

b.x: 42.6 Batch versus stream, Lambda versus Kappa

x: Batch
High throughput on complete data; results arrive after minutes or hours; simple to reason about.
Stream
Low latency on each event; must handle late, duplicate and out-of-order events; state management is harder.
Lambda architecture
Runs a batch layer (accurate, slow) and a speed layer (approximate, fast) side by side and merges their results. Powerful but you maintain two code paths.
Kappa architecture
Treats everything as a stream: keep the full log (for example in Kafka) and reprocess by replaying it with the same streaming code. Simpler, one code path.

Saying Hadoop and Spark are the same. HDFS (storage) and MapReduce (compute) are Hadoop components; Spark is a separate compute engine that can run on top of HDFS, but also on object stores and other systems.

Know the three Hadoop-era words (HDFS, MapReduce, YARN as the resource manager), the word-count trace, why Spark is faster for iterative work (memory plus lineage), and Kafka's topic, partition, offset and consumer group.

sec.t: Vector Databases and AI-Era Data Systems
sec.s: Embeddings, similarity search, approximate nearest-neighbour indexes and retrieval-augmented generation.

b.x: 43.1 Why a new kind of database?

Classic databases answer exact questions: 'find the row where id = 5' or 'find names that start with As'. Modern AI applications need similarity questions: 'find documents that mean the same as this question' or 'find images like this one'. Such meaning cannot be matched with equality or keywords. Vector databases store and search embeddings to answer them.
43.2 Embeddings

An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector, commonly 384 to 3072 dimensions) produced by a machine learning model so that items with similar meaning end up close together in the vector space. Text, images and audio can all be embedded. Two sentences about the same topic have nearby vectors even if they share no words.
43.3 Similarity measures

x: Cosine similarity  cos(a, b) = (a · b) / (|a| x |b|)       angle between the vectors, range -1 to 1
Euclidean (L2)     d(a, b) = sqrt( sum (ai - bi)^2 )           straight-line distance, smaller is closer
Inner product      a · b = sum (ai x bi)                       larger is more similar (equals cosine when vectors are normalised)
cos(a, b) = 29.5 / (3.742 x 7.971) = 0.9993   (almost the same direction)
cos(a, c) = 1 / (3.742 x 3.162) = 0.0845     (nearly perpendicular, unrelated)
So b is much more similar to a than c is. Notice L2 alone is less clear than cosine here because b is also longer than a; cosine ignores length and compares direction.

b.x: 43.4 Exact versus approximate nearest-neighbour search

Exact search compares the query vector with every stored vector: correct but cost grows linearly with the data, impractical for millions of vectors at low latency. Approximate nearest-neighbour (ANN) indexes give up a little accuracy (recall) for a very large speed-up. The key trade-off is recall versus latency versus memory.
43.5 ANN index families

x: HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)

A layered proximity graph. The sparse upper layers have long links for fast coarse navigation, like express trains; the dense bottom layer holds all vectors with short links. A search enters at the top, greedily moves towards the query and descends layer by layer. Parameters: M (links per node; more means better recall but more memory), ef_construction (candidates examined while building; better graph but slower build) and ef_search (candidates examined at query time; higher recall but higher latency). Fast and accurate, but memory-hungry.
IVF (inverted file)

Vectors are clustered into lists around centroids. A query is compared with centroids and only the nearest few lists are scanned (the nprobe setting). Cheaper to build and smaller than HNSW; recall drops if few lists are probed, and the clustering may need rebuilding when the data distribution drifts.
Product quantization (PQ)

Compresses each vector into short codes by splitting it into sub-vectors and replacing each with the id of the nearest centroid. Saves memory enormously at some cost in accuracy; often combined with IVF.
Flat (exact)
No index. Best for small collections or as ground truth to measure recall.

b.x: 43.6 Vectors inside a relational database: pgvector
Vectors do not require a separate product. The PostgreSQL extension pgvector adds a vector column type, distance operators and indexes.

x: -- PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension
CREATE EXTENSION vector;
CREATE TABLE doc (id serial PRIMARY KEY, body text, emb vector(3));
INSERT INTO doc (body, emb) VALUES ('db notes', '[1,2,3]'), ('cooking', '[3,-1,0]');
CREATE INDEX ON doc USING hnsw (emb vector_cosine_ops);   -- or ivfflat
-- three nearest documents to a query vector (<=> is cosine distance)
SELECT id, body FROM doc ORDER BY emb <=> '[2,4,6.5]' LIMIT 3;
-- combine with ordinary filters (metadata filtering)
SELECT id, body FROM doc WHERE lang = 'en' ORDER BY emb <=> '[2,4,6.5]' LIMIT 3;

b.x: Keeping vectors in the same database as the rest of the data gives transactions, joins, access control and backups for free. Dedicated vector databases (for example Milvus, Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone) offer features such as distributed indexes, and several general databases have added vector search too: Apache Cassandra 5.0 (storage-attached indexes with a vector type), MongoDB (Atlas Vector Search) and others.
43.7 Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)
Large language models know only what they were trained on and can state wrong facts. RAG lets them answer from your own documents. The pipeline:

x: 1. Chunk    split documents into passages (for example 300 to 800 words)
2. Embed    convert each chunk to a vector with an embedding model
3. Store    save chunk text + vector + metadata in a vector index
4. Retrieve embed the question; find the top-k most similar chunks
5. Generate give the question and those chunks to the language model
and ask it to answer using them (and to cite them)
Hybrid search combines vector similarity with keyword search (BM25 or full-text) because exact names, codes and rare terms are matched better by keywords; the two rankings are merged.
Metadata filtering restricts retrieval by user, date, language or permission before or during the vector search.
Re-ranking applies a more precise model to the top candidates.

b.x: 43.8 Limitations and cautions

x: Recall versus latency: ANN may miss the true nearest neighbours; measure recall against an exact search on a sample.
Memory cost: HNSW indexes for large collections need much RAM; quantization or disk-based indexes reduce it.
Index maintenance: updates and deletes are more costly than for B-trees, and IVF may need retraining.
Model dependence: changing the embedding model means re-embedding the whole collection, because vectors from different models are not comparable.

Security and privacy: embeddings can leak information about the original text; apply the same access control, encryption and retention rules as to the source data, and enforce permissions during retrieval so that users only retrieve what they may see (Topics 32 and 34).
Quality: retrieval quality depends on chunking and the embedding model, not only on the database.
Treating similarity scores as truth. High similarity means 'close in the model's space', not 'correct'. Always evaluate retrieval with real questions.
Define embedding, name the metrics (cosine, L2, inner product), explain why exact search does not scale, describe HNSW and IVF in two lines each, and draw the RAG pipeline.

sec.s: Hash pointers, Merkle trees, consensus, smart contracts, and a hash-chained audit table you can run.

b.x: 44.1 Beyond the introduction

Topics 22 to 25 of the base notes introduced blockchain as a decentralized ledger. This topic looks inside: the cryptographic structures that make it tamper-evident, how nodes agree, and how to use the same ideas in an ordinary database.
44.2 Hash pointers and the chain

A cryptographic hash function (for example SHA-256) maps any input to a fixed-size fingerprint. It is one-way and changing even one character of the input changes the hash completely. Each block stores the hash of the previous block (a hash pointer). Changing an old block changes its hash, which no longer matches the pointer stored in the next block; fixing that changes the next block's hash and so on, so a tamperer must recompute the entire chain, and in a public blockchain redo the consensus work for every later block.

x: Block 1            Block 2            Block 3
[prev: 000..0]     [prev: H(B1)]      [prev: H(B2)]
[merkle root]      [merkle root]      [merkle root]

b.x: 44.3 Merkle trees

The transactions of a block are summarised in a Merkle tree: each leaf is the hash of a transaction, each internal node is the hash of its two children, and the top is the Merkle root stored in the block header. Any change to any transaction changes the root. A light client can verify that a transaction is in a block with only a short proof (one hash per tree level), without downloading the whole block.

b.h: Worked example with four transactions (SHA-256, first 8 hex digits shown)
x: T1 = 'A pays B 5'   T2 = 'B pays C 2'   T3 = 'C pays D 1'   T4 = 'D pays A 3'
Leaf hashes:  H1 = df6a3601   H2 = c075f177   H3 = b25bc6d2   H4 = 24e83144
Tamper: change T2 to 'B pays C 9'. H2 changes, so H12 changes, so the root changes to e925cbee. The block header no longer matches.

Proof that T3 is in the block: give H4 and H12. The verifier computes H3, then H34 = H(H3 + H4), then the root = H(H12 + H34) and compares it with the header: only two extra hashes for four transactions; for a million transactions, about 20.

b.x: 44.4 Consensus: proof of work and proof of stake

x: Proof of work (PoW)

Miners repeatedly hash the block header with different nonce values until the hash is below a target. Finding one is costly, checking is cheap. The chain with the most accumulated work wins. Security comes from the cost of out-computing the honest majority; the drawback is huge energy use and low throughput. Used by Bitcoin.
Proof of stake (PoS)

Validators lock up (stake) coins and are chosen to propose and vote on blocks, with misbehaviour punished by losing the stake. Much less energy; security comes from economic penalties. Used by Ethereum since 2022.
Permissioned consensus
In a private consortium the participants are known, so faster protocols (for example Raft or Byzantine fault tolerant voting) are enough.

b.x: 44.5 Forks and finality

If two miners find a block at almost the same time, the chain temporarily forks. Nodes follow the longest (heaviest) chain, so the shorter branch is abandoned and its transactions return to the pool. Therefore a transaction is only probabilistically final in PoW: each additional block on top makes it less likely to be reversed. Some PoS systems add explicit finality: after enough validators vote, a block cannot be reverted without destroying a large amount of stake.
44.6 Smart contracts

A smart contract is a program stored on the blockchain whose execution is replicated and verified by every node, so its outcome is the same for everyone and cannot be changed after deployment. Contracts hold and move digital assets according to code ('if payment arrives, release the item'). Strengths: automation without a trusted intermediary. Weaknesses: bugs are permanent and have caused large losses, they cannot access outside data without an 'oracle', and every operation costs fees.
44.7 Public versus permissioned blockchains

x: Public (Bitcoin, Ethereum)
Anyone can join and read; strong censorship resistance; slow and costly; pseudonymous.
Permissioned (for example Hyperledger Fabric)
Only vetted members join; higher throughput; privacy through channels; suited to consortia such as supply chains. It is a shared database with cryptographic audit rather than an open currency system.

b.x: 44.8 A tamper-evident audit table in SQLite
You do not need a blockchain to get tamper evidence inside one database. A hash chain makes each audit row depend on the previous one. The script below runs in Python's sqlite3 module.

x: import sqlite3, hashlib
db = sqlite3.connect(':memory:')
db.execute('CREATE TABLE audit(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, event TEXT, prev_hash TEXT, hash TEXT)')
def add(event, prev):
h = hashlib.sha256((prev + event).encode()).hexdigest()
db.execute('INSERT INTO audit(event, prev_hash, hash) VALUES (?,?,?)', (event, prev, h))
return h
prev = '0' * 64                      # genesis value
for e in ['login asha', 'update marks 7', 'logout asha']:
prev = add(e, prev)
def verify():
for id_, event, ph, h in db.execute('SELECT id, event, prev_hash, hash FROM audit ORDER BY id'):
if ph != prev or hashlib.sha256((ph + event).encode()).hexdigest() != h:
return id_                # first broken row
prev = h
return None                       # chain is intact
print(verify())                       # None
db.execute("UPDATE audit SET event = 'update marks 99' WHERE id = 2")
print(verify())                       # 2

b.x: After the update, row 2 no longer matches its stored hash, so verify() returns 2, the first broken row. Anyone changing a past event must recompute every later hash. To make this robust the latest hash must be stored (or signed) somewhere the attacker cannot rewrite, for example printed on a report, written to a write-once store or sent to an external timestamp service. Some databases offer built-in 'ledger tables' with this behaviour.
44.9 When blockchain is NOT the right tool

x: There is one trusted owner of the data: use a normal database with good access control and a hash-chained audit log.
You need high write throughput, low latency or large data: blockchains are slow and storage-hungry.
You must be able to delete or correct data (privacy laws such as the right to erasure): immutability conflicts with that.
Participants already trust a central authority.
A blockchain may make sense when several parties who do not fully trust each other must share one authoritative record and no one wants to be the central owner.

Saying blockchain data can never be changed. Honest statement: it is tamper-evident and very expensive to change after enough blocks, but not physically impossible, and mistakes written to it also stay there.

sec.t: Data Governance, Metadata and Data Quality
sec.s: Who owns the data, how it is described and tracked, and how its quality is measured and kept high.

b.x: 45.1 What is data governance?

Data governance is the set of policies, roles and processes that make sure data is accurate, secure, available and used properly throughout its life. Security protects data from the wrong people; governance asks the wider questions: who is responsible for this data, what does it mean, how good is it, how long do we keep it and who may use it for which purpose.
45.2 Metadata, data dictionary and catalog

x: Technical metadata
Table and column names, types, constraints, indexes, sizes, storage location.
Business metadata
What a column means in business terms, units, allowed values, owner, sensitivity label (public, internal, personal, confidential).
Operational metadata
When and by which job data was loaded, row counts, run times, errors.
Data dictionary

A document or catalog table describing each table and column. Every relational DBMS has a system catalog (for example sqlite_master in SQLite, information_schema in PostgreSQL and MySQL) that stores technical metadata.
Data catalog
A searchable inventory of an organisation's data sets with descriptions, owners, lineage and quality scores, so people can find and trust data.
-- technical metadata in SQLite
SELECT name, type FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table';
PRAGMA table_info(student);      -- column names, types, NOT NULL, default, key
-- PostgreSQL / MySQL
SELECT column_name, data_type, is_nullable
FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'student';

b.x: 45.3 Data lineage

Lineage records where data came from and what happened to it: source system, each transformation, and the reports that use it. It lets you trace a wrong number in a report back to its cause, assess the impact of changing a source column, and prove compliance with a regulation by showing where personal data flows.
45.4 Master data management and roles

x: Master data management (MDM): keeping one authoritative version ('golden record') of core entities such as customers, products and suppliers that appear in many systems, matching and merging duplicates.
Data owner: a business leader accountable for a data domain and its rules.
Data steward: day-to-day guardian who defines meanings, monitors quality and resolves issues.
Data custodian: the technical team (DBAs) who store, secure and back up the data.

b.x: 45.5 Data quality dimensions

x: Accuracy
Does the value reflect reality? (a student's CGPA is 8.6, not 86).
Completeness
Are required values present? (no missing email).
Consistency
Is the same fact the same everywhere? (department code spelled the same in all tables).
Timeliness
Is the data up to date enough for its use?
Uniqueness
Is each real-world entity stored once? (no duplicate students).
Validity
Does the value follow the rules for format, range and domain? (CGPA between 0 and 10).

b.x: 45.6 Measuring quality with SQL

Quality rules can be written as queries that find violations. Test data: student rows (1 Asha asha@x.in 8.6 CSE), (2 Ravi NULL 7.2 ECE), (3 Meera asha@x.in 11.5 CSE), (4 Karan karan@x.in 6.9 XYZ) and a duplicate of row 4, and a department table that lists only CSE and ECE.

x: -- completeness: how many emails are missing?
SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, SUM(email IS NULL) AS null_email,
ROUND(100.0 * SUM(email IS NULL) / COUNT(*), 1) AS pct_null
FROM student;                          -- 5 | 1 | 20.0
-- uniqueness: duplicate roll numbers
SELECT roll, COUNT(*) FROM student GROUP BY roll HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;   -- roll 4: 2
-- uniqueness: shared emails
SELECT email, COUNT(*) FROM student WHERE email IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY email HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;    -- asha@x.in: 2, karan@x.in: 2
-- validity: CGPA outside 0..10
SELECT roll, cgpa FROM student WHERE cgpa < 0 OR cgpa > 10;      -- roll 3: 11.5
-- consistency / referential: department code not in the dept table
SELECT DISTINCT dept FROM student
WHERE dept NOT IN (SELECT code FROM dept);                       -- XYZ

b.x: The best fix is prevention: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK (cgpa BETWEEN 0 AND 10) and FOREIGN KEY constraints reject bad data at the door. Queries like the ones above remain useful to audit legacy and loaded data.
45.7 Retention, archival and privacy

x: Retention policy: how long each class of data is kept (for example financial records for the legally required years, logs for a set period).
Archival: move old, rarely used data to cheaper storage but keep it retrievable.

Disposal: delete or anonymise when the retention period ends or purpose is fulfilled. This connects directly to the storage-limitation and erasure duties under India's DPDP Act and under GDPR (Topic 34).
Classification drives controls: personal and sensitive data get encryption, masking and stricter access (Topic 32).

b.x: 45.8 Data observability

Observability applies the monitoring ideas of Topic 11 to data pipelines: track freshness (did last night's load arrive?), volume (row counts within the normal range?), schema changes, distribution drift and failed quality checks, and alert the owner before users see wrong reports.

x: Treating governance as a one-time documentation project. Without named owners, regular checks and automatic alerts, dictionaries and policies go out of date within months.

b.x: 46.1 k-anonymity check
A hospital wants to publish a table. ZIP code and age are quasi-identifiers (they can be combined with outside data to re-identify people). Original data and the generalised version:

x: Original                          Generalised (ZIP to 4 digits + *, age to decade)
ZIP    Age  Disease               ZIP    Age  Disease
47906  29   Heart                 4790*  2*   Heart
47677  35   Cancer                4767*  3*   Cancer
47602  36   Cancer                4767*  3*   Cancer
47678  32   Cancer                4767*  3*   Cancer

b.x: Group the generalised rows by the quasi-identifiers (ZIP, age): the group (4790*, 2*) has 3 rows and the group (4767*, 3*) has 3 rows. The smallest group has 3 rows, so the table is 3-anonymous: an attacker who knows a person's ZIP and age can narrow them down only to a group of at least 3.

But look at the second group: all three have Cancer. An attacker who knows someone is in group (4767*, 3*) learns their disease with certainty (a homogeneity attack). The table is 3-anonymous but not 2-diverse for that group; l-diversity requires at least l different sensitive values in each group. Therefore stronger protection needs either more generalisation or removing the group.
46.2 Quorum calculations

x: N = 5 replicas.
W = 3, R = 3:  R + W = 6 > 5, so every read overlaps the latest write.
Writes succeed with up to 2 replicas down (need 3 of 5);
reads also succeed with up to 2 replicas down.
W = 2, R = 3:  R + W = 5, not greater than 5. The 2 replicas that took the write
and the 3 replicas that are read can be completely different
sets, so a read may return stale data.
W = 5, R = 1:  R + W = 6 > 5. Reads are fast and see the latest value, but a
single failed replica blocks all writes.

b.x: 46.6 Cosine similarity

Vectors u = (1, 0) and v = (1, 1). u · v = 1 x 1 + 0 x 1 = 1. |u| = 1, |v| = sqrt(2) = 1.414. cos(u, v) = 1 / 1.414 = 0.7071, an angle of 45 degrees. Multiplying v by 10 gives (10, 10) with the same cosine 0.7071 but a much larger Euclidean distance: cosine ignores length.
46.7 Merkle proof

A block has four transactions T1 to T4 with leaf hashes H1 to H4, internal hashes H12 = H(H1 + H2) and H34 = H(H3 + H4), and root R = H(H12 + H34). To prove that T3 is in the block a full node sends H4 and H12. The verifier recomputes H3 from T3, then H34 = H(H3 + H4), then R' = H(H12 + H34) and accepts if R' equals the root in the block header. Two hashes were enough instead of all four transactions; a block of 1,048,576 (2 to the power 20) transactions needs only 20.

b.x: 48.1 Questions with answers

x: 1. Explain the Bell-LaPadula model.

It is a mandatory access control model for confidentiality. Subjects have clearance levels and objects have classifications. The simple security property says a subject may not read an object at a higher level (no read up), and the star property says it may not write to a lower level (no write down), so information cannot flow from high to low.
2. How does ABAC differ from RBAC?

RBAC decides by the role a user holds. ABAC evaluates a policy on attributes of the user, the resource, the action and the environment, for example allow if user.department = record.department and time is in office hours. ABAC is more flexible and fine-grained but harder to administer and audit.
3. What is the inference problem in statistical databases?

Users who may only ask aggregate queries can still deduce individual values by combining queries or using small query sets, such as asking for the average salary of the group of one person. Defences include minimum query-set size, restricting overlapping queries, adding noise and differential privacy.
4. Define k-anonymity and give its weakness.

A table is k-anonymous if every combination of quasi-identifier values is shared by at least k rows, so a person is hidden among k candidates. Its weakness is that all rows in a group may share the same sensitive value (homogeneity attack), which l-diversity addresses.
5. Name key obligations of a data fiduciary under India's DPDP Act, 2023.

Give clear notice and obtain valid consent (or rely on a permitted legitimate use), process data only for the stated purpose, keep it accurate, apply reasonable security safeguards, report personal data breaches to the Data Protection Board and affected persons, erase data when the purpose ends, and obtain verifiable parental consent for children under 18. Significant data fiduciaries have extra duties. Check the current text of the Act and Rules for the exact timeline.
6. Compare Redis, MongoDB, Cassandra and Neo4j in one line each.

Redis is an in-memory key-value store for caches and sessions; MongoDB stores flexible documents with rich queries; Cassandra is a partitioned wide-column store with very high write throughput; Neo4j is a graph database for relationship traversals.
7. When should data be embedded and when referenced in MongoDB?

Embed when the child data is always read with the parent, is small and bounded, and belongs to one parent (order lines inside an order). Reference when the child data is large, unbounded, shared by many parents or updated independently, because embedding would duplicate or bloat documents.
8. What is a quorum and what does R + W > N guarantee?

A quorum is the number of replicas that must acknowledge a read (R) or write (W) among N copies. If R + W > N, every read set shares at least one replica with every write set, so a read can obtain the latest acknowledged write (when versions are compared correctly).
9. State the CAP theorem and the PACELC extension.

CAP: in the presence of a network partition a distributed system must give up either consistency or availability. PACELC adds that Else, when the system runs normally, there is still a trade-off between latency and consistency, because coordinating replicas takes time.
10. Explain how consistent hashing helps when nodes change.

Keys and nodes are placed on a hash ring and each key belongs to the next node clockwise. When a node is added or removed only the keys in the neighbouring arc move, instead of almost all keys as with hash mod N. Virtual nodes smooth the load.
11. Compare B-tree and LSM-tree storage engines.

B-trees update pages in place, giving predictable reads and good range scans but random writes. LSM-trees buffer writes in a memtable, flush sorted SSTables sequentially and compact them later, giving high write throughput at the cost of read amplification and compaction work.
12. Differentiate OLTP and OLAP, and star and snowflake schemas.

OLTP handles many short transactions on normalized current data; OLAP handles complex analytical queries on historical, integrated data. A star schema has a central fact table joined to denormalized dimension tables; a snowflake schema further normalizes the dimensions into sub-tables, saving space but needing more joins.
13. Explain slowly changing dimension type 2.

When an attribute such as a customer's city changes, a new dimension row with a new surrogate key and validity dates is added and the old row is closed. Facts keep pointing to the row that was current when they happened, preserving full history.
14. Describe the MapReduce execution of word count.

Map emits (word, 1) for every word; the framework shuffles and sorts so that all pairs with the same word reach one reducer; reduce sums the values to give the count of each word. Failed tasks are simply rerun.
15. What is RAG and why use a vector database in it?

Retrieval-augmented generation first retrieves the passages most relevant to a question and then gives them to a language model as context. A vector database stores passage embeddings and finds the nearest ones to the question's embedding quickly, so the model can answer from current, private documents.
